episodes.title: Ep. 179 "Finger Exercises for Poets" by Dorianne Laux; "The Sullivanians" by Alexander Stille
episodes.description: Transcript: JESSICA: Hi, this is Jessica Russell. I'm the assistant director of collection services at Sno-Isle Libraries . And welcome to Book Buzz. Today's two reading recommendations are " Finger Exercises for Poets " by Dorianne Laux and " The Sullivanians " by Alexander Stille. First, we're going to hear from Kerry, cataloging and acquisitions assistant, for a book that explores a refreshingly hands-on approach to finding your poetic voice. Take it away, Kerry. KERRY: For anyone interested in learning more about poetry — in reading it or writing it — "Finger Exercises for Poets" by Dorianne Laux is a great place to start. Poetry can sometimes feel difficult — even intimidating — to get next to. This book reminds us that all great work is work-in-progress, that each step is a step in the right direction, and that the rewards of this effort can be eye-opening and profound. Laux begins with the notion that all forms of art (from piano to poetry) take practice; it takes time to study and develop your skills. Practice is an exercise in concentration, but also in curiosity, discovery, and play. Using examples from many different poets and styles of verse, Laux illustrates how any moment of working with language, form, and imagery can be surprisingly fulfilling and fruitful. Here you'll encounter poems you've never seen before and re-read familiar poems in very new ways. Most importantly, Laux also offers writing exercises which encourage you to pick up a pen and start practicing — to search and explore, to observe and reveal, to find your voice and fully experience those elusive and transformative moments of creativity through wordsmithing. For further inspiration, I also recommend "Real Toads, Imaginary Gardens" by Paisley Rekdal, "The Ode Less Travelled" by Stephen Fry, and "The Poetry Home Repair Manual" by Ted Kooser. JESSICA: Thanks, Kerry! It's always exciting to hear about a book that helps unlock creativity. Next, let's hear about the strange rise and fall of a community built around radical ideas, from Abby, librarian at the Arlington Library. Over to you, Abby. ABBY: If you enjoy a mind—bending tale about modern cults, I've got a book for you! "The Sullivanians" by Alexander Stille tells the story of the Sullivan Institute — a Manhattan group that started in the 1950s as psychoanalytic therapy became all the rage with the intellectual elites. Abstract expressionist Jackson Pollock was part of a wave of famous artists and cultural icons that were enticed to join the Sullivan Institute with the promise of communal living that would free them from traditional family structure. By the 1960s, the group lived in an urban commune of three to four hundred people who practiced polyamory and creativity hand in hand. However, by the 1970s their vision of community had warped into a mind control game of truly epic proportions. The group's leader, Saul Newton, held a strict requirement that all members attend "therapy sessions" with psychoanalysts who used these private sessions to dictate the lives of their patients with increasing intensity. Their goal was to ensure parents never raised their own biological children. Not all parents were willing to surrender their children, though, and the story of how a few key members refusing to give up their babies led to the unraveling of the Institute is truly fascinating. This story was a great look at the myriad of ways that intellectual elites can fall prey to the madness of group think. JESSICA: Thanks, Abby! That sounds like a compelling story that's as thought-provoking as it is unsettling. Our recommendations this week are: "Finger Exercises for Poets" by Dorianne Laux and "The Sullivanians" by Alexander Stille. Join us next time, when we'll explore more great reading recommendations — interesting books you can find at your favorite local bookstore or at your local library. Until then, I'm Jessica Russell from Sno-Isle Libraries. Thanks for joining us for Book Buzz.
